translations.text: Causes are what move speech, and speech is what tells of causes. For this reason they first come to the senses, and the senses bring them to the faculty that receives them,

And the receiver would give it to the examiner, and the examiner to the keeper. And so the thing that had been shaped would come back, and he would blow into the pipe [?] of his own tongue, and deliberately they would groan [?],
so that it may in turn pass to other hearers through the shared act of hearing. This is our present undertaking.
For it is right that the knowledge of the blessed ones, recorded in writing by hand, be made known as an account of those great men,
who ought to be spread abroad as preaching to the whole world by the ministers of the word, through revelation from on high; they were adorned by the revelation of the truth.
We are not looking for something easily found. We want to bring clearly into view precious pearls from the depths of the sea, which can only be won by hard work,
pearls that are ready to share out wealth, the incorruptible treasure of divine gifts, to our people through the word of grace.
Brother Michael, I have read the letter with your request and understood how eager your request is, and your love of learning pleased me greatly,
For you wanted me to write the Life of the great John of Zedazeni and send it to your desert. First,
you wished it so that the virtues of that holy father and teacher would not stay hidden in the depths. Second, you wished it so that we might gain benefit from them.
And that slender letter which you sent to us, from which I read about the deeds of our father of Zedazeni, and we examined some things concerning him and his disciples,
and about the places connected with them, just as someone might send gold dust to a craftsman so that he could gather it together and make it into a beautiful vessel.
By such eagerness you do not receive anything from us. Rather, you give, just as the Lord of glory, when he came to the well, asked the Samaritan woman for water.
He was not receiving; he was granting her the spring of life. In the same way, I am the one who receives, not the one who gives to you.
But when I saw this good guest who had come to me, I ran out with joy and brought him up into my chamber, and I wanted to satisfy the hunger he was seeking to fill.
when I opened my treasury, I found it lacking and meagre because of my small knowledge. And since I am slow of tongue and not eloquent, where could I begin to tell of that saint's virtues?
But I decided to be like the hard-working bee and to gather flowers from the beautiful paradises of books, so that
it might prepare sweet food for those who long for it, to our glory. But it is right that we first begin with prayer. Join your hands with me in supplication!
For prayer is what makes all good things fragrant. Prayer nourished Samuel in his mother's womb and revealed him as a prophet.
See the fruit of prayer: he became a prophet of the truth from his childhood, because Hannah asked for him with tears and prayer.
Likewise, when the lawgiver Moses was about to receive the tablets of the law, he laid forty days of prayer and fasting as the foundation. And the tablets of Moses, written by the finger of God,
he brought down from the mountain once, and a second time to complete the work. For the first tablets were broken, as being Jewish [?], but the second were honoured through the change,
Therefore it is fitting that everyone who undertakes divine service should ask of him who is God, the generous bestower, and he will give nourishment, as James the apostle says:
"If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask, and God, the distributor of gifts, will give it to him."
At the beginning of [a work on] the writers, it is right to make mention of the great Moses, who began the house [?] by writing, the one who signified the truth beforehand,
he who, like Noah's ark, was carried on the water, armed by glory [?], cast out through fear,
was rescued by the efforts of God [literally "of gods"]. He was nourished by Pharaoh's daughter in the very house of that same king. He killed the Egyptian,
Pharaoh's son-in-law, who was not distant or obscure but close to Pharaoh, since he was a figure of all of the truth:
the first [Moses], [a figure] of the new law; that son-in-law of Pharaoh, [a figure] of the Pharaoh of the incorporeal Pharaoh, as Egypt [is a figure] of hell, each close to the other in figure [?].
He became a fugitive from the king's wrath and went out into the desert to Mount Sinai.
The angel of God appeared in fire within the bush, the mystery of the Virgin, and in astonishment he came to see.
He was called by him, and while living he stripped the skin of the dead [animal] from his feet and presented himself for the revelation.
He was the one who was attested by that same Most High to be the god of Pharaoh, the ruler of darkness and apostate from the supreme good. He,
who became higher than the loftiest summits of the high mountains, the figure of the giver of the true law! Him he sent to deliver Israel with wonders and signs.
But the one who sends revealed himself, who he was, and said:
"I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob," and of the one who made [things] known to your fathers [?].
He made his name known from the mountain [?] to the three patriarchs, the great and righteous ones; he was named God. Then Moses, the one who received [it], asks God again:
"If they say to me, 'Who sent you?', what shall I say?" He taught him to speak of that one bottomless depth, and said to him: "Say this: 'He who is sent me.'
He is the One who is, who has no beginning." And as proof he gave him those ten very great signs, by which he is the God of the fathers,
so that they might believe the boundary of the knowledge of the true God, that great light. [But] darkness seized them, and they were swallowed up in the deep.
And the one who is that light is the one invisible and unchangeable God, without beginning and without end, immeasurable,
ever blessed, the light of the Trinity, for this [light] of the most divine Godhead [?] unites the three hypostases together: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
is in this way counted as united, unconfused and undivided. It is not right to make the Son less than the Father, or the Spirit less than the Son. And
if the Godhead were not like this, it would not be so very glorious. For it is invisible, timeless, uncontainable and unchangeable, unchangeable and without quality,
without quantity and without form, incomprehensible and indivisible. It moves itself with an everlasting motion and is powerful in itself. Although everything is drawn toward the first cause,
which belongs to him as the Son, the only one who is living and life-giving, the giver of life, as he says:
"I live, and you too shall live, and whoever believes in me shall also live through me,"
that light, ever blessed and radiant, not separate from the supreme nature of being, an everlasting light [?] by hearing [?].
And the Holy Spirit, Lord of sovereignty, who sends forth and apportions, who makes for himself a temple as he wills and in whomever he wills.
For the Spirit gives and creates and is not created. Through him was established that created light of the second radiances, I mean that of the angels,
and the third light, this heaven. Both have their beginning from that first light, the source, from which come the three, and from the three one, but only this:

for the Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Father, and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son. And this does not divide the nature; rather, there is distinction within the nature, and it points to unity.
But those who have not understood the equality of the Trinity are in darkness and stumble. Let them be ashamed of Arius,
He presumed to call the Word of God created, though it was God's own Word and not another's,
and this happened because he did not understand the limits of his person and his nature. He saw him as a man, and he did not recognise the beginningless nature of the Godhead.
Again, there are the Arians too. They say that Christ was the Word of God, but they also counted the Spirit among created things, and they say that God created the Word just as he created Adam,
for [?] — you most senseless of all men — if he was God's Word, how could part of his Godhead be without beginning and part created?
Whatever a builder makes, whether a pillar or a temple, is not called the word of that builder; it is called something made by a word.
So how could Christ be the Word of God, and that Word also be created?! Their own words condemn them!
If the Word was not with Him, did the beginningless one create him later?! Was God then wordless at first, by your account?!
And again, all who do not accept the equality of the Holy Trinity ought to answer the one who asks them: can God receive an accident, or not?
If he admits that God cannot receive an accident, let us ask: is the Word of God an accident, or not?
If he says it is an accident, I would be denying what I have confessed.
But God forbid that something which did not exist before should have entered into God, which would be the case if He were shown to receive accidents,
for everything that receives accidents increases and decreases. And how can anyone say of God that He increases and decreases?
It remains that it should be a brand [?], for everything is divided into two: the brand [?] and the completed [?],
and whatever is not completed [?] is clearly a brand [?]. And things that are a brand [?] stand by themselves.
But that which is of God is the Creator and not something created. I speak of the Word without beginning, through whom God created everything that is created.
And it cannot be otherwise, for everything is divided into two kinds: the created and the Creator.
It is also clear which is the Creator and which is created. The Word is not created. To put it briefly, there is nothing among created things that could be a creator.
I say the same about the Holy Spirit too. But Macedonius dared to count the Holy Spirit among created things
and to say that the sovereign Holy Spirit is sent by grace. He was a bold and self-willed man, who thought himself to be something that he was not.
He strengthened his tongue to fight against God, even after hearing that fearful saying:
"All sins and blasphemies will be forgiven to men, but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven."
and he did not understand that saying of the prophet David:
"By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power."
If the Spirit is of his mouth, how could that Holy Spirit be created!
For all that exists is his. If the Spirit was created, then the Father must somehow have been without a Spirit until that Spirit was created!
Rather, its Creator is that Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father and is worshipped together with the Son,
That Spirit which moved over the waters, and by that movement over them gave shape to and created all creatures, and by grace brought forth each one as he willed.
That Spirit came down on the apostles like fire, and with surpassing wonder divided tongues among them.
Behold, a grace beyond words: the apostle speaks in Hebrew, in one tongue only, and all the barbarians hear him in every tongue!
May the spirit of wisdom, knowledge and understanding come on us from this Spirit, and may our tongue be given the grace to find words,
so that I may speak without error about holy John Zedazneli and honour him, for the benefit of the zealous [?] of the desert.
As for you, make your ears ready and receive this with faith. Do not think that you have heard about all the virtue of this man. Because of the constraints of time, this is only a little out of much.
This blessed John came from the land of Mesopotamia. Guided by the Holy Spirit, he came to the land of Kartli,
near this capital city of ours, Mtskheta. He had dedicated himself to Christ from his childhood.
From his youth he took up the heavy yoke. He sat alone and kept silence, for there is hope in endurance.
He first began to live as a monk in his own land, Assyria.
He lived in all humility, with fasting and vigils, with tears and supplication. Through labour and endurance he advanced day by day,
so that he might attain the perfection that he would receive, of which it says: "Knock and it will be opened to you; seek and you will find."
Once he was enlightened, he first attained that glory, and he saw what was far away as though it were near. He shone like a star.
The powers worked by him through God multiplied: healings of many kinds of disease, and the casting out of demons.
Then he left the place where they were living and went into a remote desert. He found a cave there and settled in it with his disciples,
and for a long time no one knew of that place. Only rarely would he send one of his disciples to fetch food.
So he lived there in secret, thinking he was hiding himself.
But afterward God also made his servant known, for this is God's custom:
"Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted." People began once again to come to him there too,
though he was hidden in the cave. They brought the sick on beds, people struck by all kinds of afflictions, and they found relief there at once.
In saying this, brethren, I am not telling you about his deeds there or about his life. Rather, I am recounting to you the reason why he came to this land of ours.
For the earlier life and deeds of this blessed man are written in the first book, and it is blessed [?] for us to write them down a second time.
Then the blessed John began to consider in his mind going away to a distant land,
where no word at all of his virtues had been heard. And he said: "From where should I guard myself? It is necessary that his journey be made to prosper [?]."
But while he was only thinking about this, his guide, the Holy Spirit, pointed him toward the northern land, so that it might lead him to the land of Kartli.
It was he who wished to come here, but another was the one who brought him: the same one who once called Abraham and said to him:
"Go out from your land and from among your kindred, and go to the land that I will show you."
From one land and from one people he brought out Abraham and John,
for truly Saint John was one of the offspring of Abraham. Hear what the apostle Paul says:
"If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's children, heirs according to the promise." Truly a holy root has sprung up into something good.
Then the blessed John began to make his plans and said to his disciples: "Stay here, for I wish to go to a remote land, in case I may find what I am seeking."
But the blessed disciples remembered the word of the prophet Elisha:
"As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, we will not leave you alone, wherever you go."
"And the spring from which we drink every day, and by which we are satisfied, let us not deprive ourselves of it in these few days of ours."
"And what you have judged to be good for yourself, be pleased to grant to us as well."
O the good agreement of the excellent teacher's disciples! They were bound together by the bond of love, and together they pulled at the yoke of Christ.
Then he set out from his own land for the land of Kartli, guided by the invisible power that once, in the form of a star, led the Magi.
He arrived at this capital city of ours, Mtskheta. When he had paid homage at the holy churches, he went in before the holy catholic Pillar,
[The pillar] raised up by God and revealed from on high with great wonder, which was held up above the gates for a long time and which all the people of Kartli saw,
God, not man, made it firm, so that its foundations would stay unshaken forever.
whose fame spread through every land, and which all the efforts of craftsmen and kings, with a countless multitude of people, could not raise up for three days.
They used up all their strength, gave up, and went away in the evening. They took all their machines with them, and hope was lost.

On that same night, our holy and flourishing mother Nino, the source of all the good things of Kartli, kept on in prayer with tears. With every kind of supplication she asked the mighty Christ, our God, for help, and quickly
that captive woman overcame all the power of the king and all the skill of the craftsmen.
Through her prayer she obtained that living pillar. It hung in the air, raised one cubit above its base, and stood upright,
And when dawn broke, behold, King Mirian and all the multitude of Kartli arrived and saw that great wonder, the mystery from God, which was done for their salvation.
and then it slowly came down, little by little, until it was set firmly on the base prepared for it. Everyone was astonished and marvelled at that great faith,
…they glorified the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. And that renewal of the faith grew greatly among those believers,
From then on the other pillars were raised, and they built the church, of which the apostle Paul makes mention:
"How one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the church, the pillar and foundation of the truth, which was shown to angels, preached among the gentiles, and believed in the world."
Holy John hurried to stand before this pillar clothed in light, as before a wondrous and honoured place revealed by God.
He prayed to God. He lifted up his eyes and raised his hands, and he shed his precious tears before that living pillar, asking to be shown the place where he would finish his course.

Then He who does the will of those who fear Him soon showed them a certain mountain near Mtskheta, toward the east and to the north of the Living Cross, so that he would go up to the summit of that mountain and live there.
As he set out, he crossed the river Aragvi and came before the life-giving Cross,
under whose wings everyone is sheltered from every evil mishap: the light revealed from on high by a great wonder, the light confirmed by God.
and he prayed for a long time. Then he left that place and went up the high mountain called Zedazeni, where his monastery now stands,
for that place was entirely covered with tall forest. When he saw it, it pleased him, and he said:
"This is my resting place; therefore I will dwell here, for I have desired it; I will bless its wild beasts with blessing."
"As I think, O blessed one, this saying is yours: 'Who would give me wings like a dove's? I would fly up, I would rise on high, I would go away and find rest in the wilderness.'"
For the Lord settled him here for two reasons.
First, so that he and his disciples might become an adornment and crown of this city of ours, like those twelve stones honored for their appearance that were set on the tunic of Aaron,
a benefit and a healer for all who live in this city of ours and call upon them, as will be told to you a little later.
Second, the place to which he was sent had been the stronghold of the former nobles, where idolatry had been exalted.
There the nobles served demons with the smoke of sacrifices. He was sent so that the worship of God would be exalted in those same places,
he cleansed that place of the venom of the wicked demons, as Sabas once did at the place called the Castellion,
and the hosts of demons were driven away. That blessed elder prayed and pleaded with God at all times, and he stood undisturbed.
he endured all the assaults of the devil, and he entrusted himself to prayer and fasting as to the mother of wisdom.
Our holy father John wished to live alone. He longed for his own dwelling place, that city whose architect and maker is God,
the heavenly Jerusalem, to join in the festival with those who rejoice there, a seeker of the heavenly pearl together with the good merchants.
Here he put himself to death, so that he might find eternal life.
Then one day that good teacher called his disciples and said to them: "Why do you stand idle? Or
do you not know that our Lord God Jesus Christ has sent us out for the benefit of this land, because the people of this country are a new planting?
You must go out, each one of you, and strengthen the brethren
who have confessed Christ our Lord, not by word, by your teaching, but by offering your own selves as an example.
For this reason the Lord has left us mingled among the gentiles, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.
"Brothers, love nothing more than God. Despise love of money and wealth. Do not give yourselves over to luxury and gluttony, or to food,
for from luxury and food was born that disobedience of Adam which has rested on his offspring ever since. It was this that drove him out of the paradise of delights.
If he had kept the law of fasting, this thorny land would not have been given to us, and death would not have ruled over us, even though the Power from on high humbled [itself] [?].
He took on flesh, and through him we have attained that first desire of ours, something higher than paradise; we have taken from the tree of life, and so we have been given life.
We have left behind the way guarded by the cherub, we have ascended to heaven as immortals, and we have come near to God.
As for wine, I think it needless for me to speak, for it is nothing at all to do with monks, since the apostle Paul showed it to be the root and cause of debauchery when he said:
"Do not get drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery." It is a deadly poison, the mother of evil desires and the thing that stirs them up.
And in the end an evil harvest comes from that evil seed. Hate it, and do not accept these things even for a single moment.
It stripped the patriarchs, not through gluttony but through inexperience. It makes the eyes bloodshot, reddens the complexion and turns a beautiful face ugly.
What is there [?] between you and that evil lover! And if you do not put it far from you, its falseness will soon show itself in you.
My brothers, do not think little of yourselves, as if you were transient and perishable. Whatever power knows itself
knows everything. So you should know that we are beings that are immortal and imperishable, created above all created things,
and honored above visible things by an endless existence. Therefore we must guard ourselves and take care for the sake of the life to come.
"For in our small human nature he created this wide world anew, and he exalted it above that world with a rational and intelligent soul,
for he gave it a perfection that has a beginning but no end: an immortal soul.
And in this respect we have come close to the nature of the angels, while in one part we are like the perishable animals.
So man is neither an angel nor a beast, but something between them, a different creature made from the two:
he joined him into one from soul and flesh, set him in a place of battle and victory, and gave him the power of self-rule,
And he set it at the point [?] of the balance and of its mind, for this mind goes out between the two united natures. And it is the governor,
if in some way it inclines.
"if it leads [him] toward the spiritual nature, it has brought the will of the flesh into submission, which leads [?] to immortality and life.
And if it inclines and leads the soul to the will of the flesh, it enslaves the soul to death and corruption. We have these two wills set against one another, as the Apostle says:
'The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, and they are opposed to one another.' And again he says:
'I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate. If that [is] not [?], I am a witness to the law, that it is good.'
So now it is no longer I who do this, but the sin that has come to dwell in me.
For I agree with the law of God, and I see another law in my members that is set against it."
"You see how clearly the apostle tells us about the two wills set against each other and fighting:
One will was created natural; it belonged to Adam in paradise before the transgression of the commandment, while he was still spiritual and [?]. But the other one,
which settled in us after the fall, not by nature, but broken in from outside the heart through that cunning [of the deceiver].
That is why the apostle did not say: "what is created is sin, which is set against the law of my mind."
Understand from these words, brothers: if any of you gives in to those opposing forces,
It is taken captive by that hateful will. But if it does not put to death the deeds of the flesh [?], it lives spiritually, unwillingly [?].
So it is now clear that both these wills are within our power, even though the devil's will ceaselessly drags the will toward his own evil, toward the desires of the flesh.
But the same Apostle says: 'What the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh,'
"God sent his Son in the likeness of flesh," and he took on this flesh of ours without sin,
cleansed of all the error of the first Adam, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us,
"for the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life."
"And truly the mind of the flesh is death, for it urges us toward every kind of impurity.
It is not only an enemy outside, but one that is always with you, when you lie down and when you rise up, in everything you do.
Restrain it as far as you can, so that it does not dash you down with a stone. It calls you without mercy, as an enemy would.
I would rather you bridle it and put it under the will of the spirit, so that you may be like that first-created one, to whom our Lord has brought us back, for you were created great.
If somehow you keep it and do not fall to that lower place, then, since you share in the wisdom of God,
how much more is it possible for the creature together with the Creator! You are living like the angels, and mortal like the animals, lower than the lowest of the abysses and higher
so that He might be incomprehensible: greatest of all great things and least of all small things, and immortal within mortality,
"This is your twofold creation. That is why it is wonderful: it is the craftsmanship of the Wonder-worker.
At this one of the saints, the deep-speaking one, marvelled at that wondrous mingling. He wished to separate himself from something [?]
he cast away what he saw as deficient, which was not able [?]. Then he lamented, and said thus:
"O, how I have been joined I do not know, and how I am the image of God and yet mixed with clay. When it is healthy, it wages war; and when it is mortified, there is grief.
I love it as my fellow-servant, for it is a servant, and I separate myself from it as from an enemy. I flee from it as from bonds, and I am ashamed of it (or: I hold it in respect) as a co-heir.
I wish to waste it away, and there is no one to help me toward the good. From it come my tears, from it fasting,
"vigils, from it the offering of prayer and many good labors, which are not possible without the body.
For I know what I exist for, and it is right for me to rise up to my God through works.
Should I spare it, since it works together with me? Yet I do not know how I am to escape its attack, so as not to be weighed down by the fetter
that drags me down to the earth, and so fall away from God. It is a cheerful enemy and a false friend."
"O union and separation, which I fear! Should I protect what I love? I am afraid of it. Before the battle I make peace, and before making peace I fight.
He made us this way so that through the hardship [?] and battle of this flesh we might look to humility, and so that this weakness joined to us might be a lesson about our dignity,
so that you may know that we are high and low, inhabitants of light or of darkness, whichever way we lean.
This is our mixture: when we are raised up through the image, we are made small because of the earth. You have understood your union and the war within you.
Keep yourself completely steady, and do not cling to that latter, evil intention.
And see: you also have another enemy, the one who threw you down from on high and never plans anything good for you.
He supports the will of the flesh, that bodiless Pharaoh who was turned from light to darkness, against the enlightened man who has crossed the Jordan.
He binds that man to his own company in the thickness of his darkness, and forces those created free to become his slaves,
so that he might carry them off to Babylon, to hell, that devourer of many, which was drowned in the sea of fire by the coming of Christ our God,
who was born of a virgin, the second Adam, with the nature of the first Adam, only without sin.
But those who have filled themselves with light from that same Light without beginning will remain in delight and will dwell in joy without going astray,
bound fast with eagerness to that immortal life that is near, by love of that same enlightening Light, forever."
And when they had received these and many other teachings, he said to them:
"Go and strengthen the flocks of Christ." And he sent some of them to Kakheti and some to the region of Kukheti,
and some to the upper region of the country, and one to the outlying region [?], and others to the surroundings of this royal city of ours.
So they went and settled, some in wooded valleys and some on mountains, in caves and in holes in the ground.
And people came to them from every side and were edified by their words and by the deeds they did, and through them the multitude of believers was made strong.
Now the very many, countless relics of the holy martyrs which they had brought along at the coming of holy John, he kept before his eyes;
he regarded them above all treasures, as though they were many hosts standing around him. And he placed his hope in them and was comforted by them.
And truly those are great treasures, more precious than all jewels (literally 'eyes'): the bones of the martyrs, of brave knights, invincible in the contest,
who shed their blood for Him who bought us with His own blood, the bulwarks of the human race.
If anyone is in distress, he flees to them, and runs to them and is gladdened. People on land and at sea alike pray to them.

And Father John kept the relics of the saints before him. As though he were watching the day of their contest, he would contemplate them in this way and live through in his mind the tortures of each one.
Every day he suffered martyrdom and added to his labours. He would pray to them and kiss them with great longing.
Whenever he sent out his disciples, he gave them some of the relics of the holy martyrs,
so that they might have them as a protection for themselves, and might build churches in the name of each of them in the dwelling-places that would be prepared for them by the grace of God.

That blessed elder lived alone, with one servant of theirs, on that mountain in great ascetic struggle. And his prayer rose up to heaven. He purified the air [?] and would pass ten days at a time [?].
But the demons, those haters of good, who had lived on that mountain from of old,
could not endure the prayers and supplications of our father John, for these became a goad to them, like red-hot arrows.
One day all the powers of darkness were stirred up. They approached holy John and began to fight against him with many schemes.
They raged in turmoil around him and tried to frighten him. They attacked him day and night, as if they had been given some power, and they threatened to throw down that rock.
But the blessed elder armed himself with the cross of Christ and counted their illusions as nothing. "Look," he would say to them, "here I am, if you have received permission."
One day that whole multitude was stirred up and appeared openly. They surrounded blessed John and said to him: "Why have you come here?"
And one of them, the chief of the demons, called him by name: "John, why do you contend with us? Where have you come from? This place is ours, and you are not able to stay here."
"Or do you not know that this boldness of yours toward us will destroy you utterly? For you cannot stand against this whole multitude. Do not deceive yourself."
Blessed John answered and said to them: "You have never accepted any counsel for the good of our race. So how should I listen to you?
Your place is darkness. Flee there.
"O slanderer, are you not the one who took that place from me, the paradise of delight? It was mine, and you devised a scheme like this against Adam and drove him out of it.
And there was a time when we became food for death through your schemes. But God could not endure the complete dishonouring of his own image,
But he came and found him buried in the depths, and he raised him up, renewed him, and healed all your wounds.
"And now, today, you are hunted on every side by his offspring, because those gifts have spread through the whole world. There is no place for you except darkness.
By your own choice you hated the light and loved the darkness. You were an angel and became a rebel; you were one who gave praise, and you were given the name of slanderer.
"But we shall receive in full that place which you promised deceitfully, and now we shall pass from this dwelling to heaven."
And at once that great multitude fled by the power of Christ,
saying in a pitiful voice: "Woe to us, for the invoking of the name of Jesus drives us out of every place,
and gives power to those who follow Him. Let us go away and settle there among the more remote heathen."
And immediately, like a thick and dark mist, it came out of that mountain, became invisible, and headed toward the north. And blessed John gave thanks to God when he saw their fall and destruction.
All who lived around that mountain heard of this matter, and they saw the glorious wonder of the wonder-working God which had
through the prayer of our father John, who fulfils the will of those who fear him.
They had already known how wicked the demons living in that place were, and they glorified God.
The blessed old man lived alone on that mountain, and his own disciple served him.
Day by day he renewed himself. He took care not to appear before his Lord empty-handed, and every day he brought good works before him as gifts.
This mountain had once been without water, and no water at all could be found around it. The pagans who had lived in the tower before had tried many ways to get it,
but even with hard digging they could not bring up water from that dry ground.
Blessed John saw how hard his disciple worked. He carried water from the foot of the mountain and brought it up for the old man's needs.
For that place is a steep ascent on every side and a long climb. And his disciple Elias took pity on the elder; he prayed and besought his Lord to give him water close by.
Then he who gave water in the wilderness to his people Israel by the hand of Moses his servant, and who made rivers flow from the dry rock when it was struck with the rod,
He delivered the twelve tribes, the sons of Israel, that great camp, not once or twice but many times. As Paul the apostle says:
"For they drank from that spiritual rock which followed them, and that rock was Christ."
That rock was a figure of Christ, and the rod was a foreshadowing of the Cross.
And the blessed one also followed Christ completely, and Christ heard his prayer. At once, at his supplication, at the place where the Cross of Christ had been set up,
just as with the rod of Moses, he struck the dry ground with that cross instead of a rod, where no one had ever seen water, and sweet water burst forth,
cool, very beautiful and abundant. To this day it flows for those who live in that monastery, and it suffices not only for them but for a great multitude.
And when this great miracle took place, people came from every side to see it, for the inhabitants of the surrounding area knew that there had been no water in that place.
By the grace of the holy one, that spring served not only for use, but many healings also took place.
People brought the sick with all kinds of illnesses, and those possessed by demons, and all who anointed themselves from that spring were healed.
They also carried its water off to distant lands, and to this day it is of benefit to those who come with faith.
But he did not wish to build in that place; rather, he lived according to the rule of the solitary life. In the cleft of the rock he had found a small cave,
in which he completed the pilgrimage of this faithful life, "being destitute, afflicted, ill-treated, of whom this world was not worthy," and what follows.
And as the Lord multiplied miracles through him, his fame spread through the land of Kartli and shone out like the morning star,
he who had glorified God in secret. Through him [Kartli] widened its bosom and received that great light brought down from on high,
for it was not possible otherwise: no one lights a lamp and hides it under a bushel, but puts it on a lampstand, so that it may give light to people.
Even if they wish to hide themselves, it is like a perfumer who fills a flask with fragrance, puts it inside another vessel, seals it well, and hangs it up to carry wherever he wishes.
And the perfumer thinks that he keeps it hidden, yet all who come near him smell the fragrance of his ointment;
in the same way good deeds cannot be hidden, even if those who do them do not wish it.
One day his servant, the blessed deacon Elijah, went to that God-given spring to draw water.
And there by the spring stood a forest bear, huge and very terrifying. The blessed Elijah was greatly afraid, turned back, and told the great John.
He came and said to the bear: "If you have not drunk that water, drink and go away." Then he laid a command on it and said:
"In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ I tell you: you shall no longer have power to do evil or harm to the people you meet on this mountain."
When the beast received the command from the elder, it learned to harm no one.
It went on its way, and kept looking back as if at a friend speaking sweetly to it. It bowed its head and quietly showed the bearing of obedience.
And its bestial nature entirely [?], nor did it show any wish to flee, for it changed its own wickedness and was turned to good.
And through his holy prayer, to this day it goes along with whomever it meets like a gentle sheep.
And this is not surprising, for even beasts know how to show honour; they pay heed to those who govern [?] and to the light.
He who fell into the pit of the beasts and shut the mouths of the lions, which had long been deprived of food and were very hungry,
Among them he lay like an unbreakable adamant stone, and the beasts did not dare to touch him at all,
but they came up to him and licked his feet, as if they were saying: "This is not flesh that has been made food for us,"
since he did not take it upon himself to taste the foods from the royal table, but only seeds. This man ate no bread and drank no water for three weeks.
It is right for us to learn from this the honour paid to those who fast.
But that blessed elder, by his own hard labour of fasting, was not content merely to drive that flesh-eating beast away from himself,
But like an apostle he was sent to his own apostles [?], kinsmen and friends, for the offspring of the offspring of their kin [?], so that they would harm no one;
and that commandment became a bridle for them [?] (poloṭik [?]), and he softened their teeth, and they live on that mountain to this very day and harm no one.
I am ashamed and grieved when I hear how a beastly nature, speechless and senseless, heeded the word of the saints,
while we have shown ourselves more wicked than beasts. We read about what happened among them [?], and we hear the commandments that were given, yet we do not stop harming our neighbours.
We abstain from eating meat, yet we chew the flesh of our neighbour. Shall we then resemble those beasts, and not flesh-
-eating men? We have received the commandment from God to love our neighbour as ourselves,
but we have made him hated along with ourselves, for hatred of one's neighbour is hatred of oneself. The one who lures us into this is envy.
O envious one, turn away from envy! Envy is death. Flee from it, so that you may not die.
Do not envy those who have advanced in the virtues, and confess that you are envious. Envy is praised [?]: that love for death [?].
For life, this is a deliverer and [?], which wears down the minds of those who think of it. But devote yourself [?] to the Scriptures and find deliverance,
and imitate those who have been perfected in virtue. Do not envy, so that you may escape a little from the snare of the enemy
and return again to the place from which you were brought down [?].
